body.heading: A basket, not a ban
paragraphs: Confiscation breeds resistance; a basket is just furniture. Phones go in the basket by the door for an agreed hour — during dinner, during the film, during the first hour of the evening — and come out again without ceremony when the hour ends.

Everyone's phone goes in, including the person who suggested it. The basket works because it is visibly fair, and because it is physical: a phone in another room stops glowing at the edge of your attention in a way a muted phone in a pocket does not.

body.heading: Choose the hour together
paragraphs: Let the household pick which hour matters most. Dinner is the classic candidate, but some families would rather protect the hour before bed, or weekend breakfast. The protected hour should be one people actually miss each other in.

Expect the first ten minutes to feel itchy. Hands reach for pockets that are empty. It passes, and what replaces it — finishing sentences, noticing the food, a conversation that wanders — is the entire point.

body.heading: Keep an emergency door open
paragraphs: Agree the exceptions in advance: the phone that might ring about a relative in hospital, the on-call job. A basket with agreed exceptions is a tool; a basket with none becomes a rule people quietly break.
After a few weeks, most households stop watching the clock. The basket stops being a rule and becomes simply where phones live during dinner.

description: An agreed hour with all phones resting in a basket by the door gives a household its attention back, fairly and physically.
